name: Bisdisulizole disodium

lead: Bisdisulizole disodium is a water-soluble UVA filter sold by Symrise as Neo Heliopan AP. It lets formulators make light, easy-to-wear sun protection against the UVA rays tied to wrinkles and dark spots.

It absorbs UVA radiation in the sunscreen formulation. It has been approved in the EU at up to 10% since 2000; few sources document it in detail, and the evidence is regulatory and formulation-based rather than appearance trials.

paras: It appears in EU sunscreens and facial SPF products with light textures suited to daily wear, typically alongside other filters that cover UVB. It is not approved in the US.
No dedicated safety information was found in the sources reviewed, and it is not approved in the United States.

angle.text: Bisdisulizole disodium (Neo Heliopan AP) is a water-soluble UVA filter in EU sunscreens. It allows light textures that suit daily facial wear and protect against UVA-linked wrinkles and dark spots. Evidence is regulatory and formulation-based rather than appearance trials.

lead: Bisdisulizole disodium (trade name Neo Heliopan AP, from Symrise; INCI name disodium phenyl dibenzimidazole tetrasulfonate, also abbreviated DPDT) is a water-soluble organic UVA filter used in sunscreens.[1] It helps skin look younger for longer by contributing UVA protection: UVA is the part of sunlight associated with photoaging, and sunscreen use has been linked to smoother, more resilient skin in studies described in Wikipedia's sunscreen article.[1][2]

Chemically it is a disodium salt of a sulfonated bis-benzimidazole, which makes it water-soluble and suited to the water phase of lightweight sunscreen formulations.[1] It is approved in the European Union since 2000 and in other regions at up to 10% in sunscreen formulations, and it is not approved in the United States.[1]

The US difference reflects how sunscreens are regulated: the US treats them as over-the-counter drugs, which slows approval of new filters, while the EU treats them as cosmetics; as of 2023 the US had 17 approved filters against 29 in the EU.[2]

paras: It absorbs UVA radiation and is used in sunscreen products, notably in water-based phases of formulations [1].
UVA radiation (315 to 400 nm) causes invisible skin damage, and SPF ratings measure protection against UVB rather than UVA. Broad-spectrum sunscreen combines UVA and UVB filters.[2]

Wikipedia's sunscreen article describes a 2013 Australian study of about 900 people in which daily broad-spectrum sunscreen over roughly four and a half years was followed by smoother, more resilient skin, and a smaller study in which daily SPF 30 use reversed signs of photoaging over 12 weeks. These studies concern sunscreens in general, not bisdisulizole disodium specifically.[2]
EU approval began in 2000 with a 10% limit; the US has not approved it [1]. The USAN Council adopted the nonproprietary name in April 2006 [1].
The formula is C20H12N4Na2O12S4, with a molar mass of about 674.55 g/mol, and the nonproprietary name was adopted in 2006.[1]
No studies found on bisdisulizole disodium alone. Research on sunscreens generally is summarised in Wikipedia's sunscreen article.[2]
